---
title: "Why measure what people don't know they want"
description: "A short first post on implicit motives — and a template you can copy for the next one."
author: "Cafer Bakaç"
date: "2026-08-15"
categories:
  - Implicit Motives
  - Notes
---

Ask people what motivates them at work and they will tell you something coherent: autonomy,
impact, recognition, a fair salary. Those answers are explicit motives, and they are real —
they predict the goals people set and the jobs they apply for.

They are also incomplete. Alongside those conscious preferences sits a second system:
affective preferences that develop early, operate outside awareness, and predict a different
class of outcomes — spontaneous behavior, persistence, and how energizing an activity feels
rather than how sensible it seems. The two systems correlate weakly at best. A person can
sincerely want a leadership role while their implicit power motive is low, and the mismatch
shows up later as fatigue rather than as a change of mind.

That gap is the part of my work I find most interesting. It is not that people misreport
their motives; it is that self-report can only reach one of the two systems. Which raises a
practical problem: the indirect measures that reach the other one are expensive to score,
which is why motive research has stayed small-sample for decades. Whether large language
models can change that is the question I am working on now.
